reason: Throughout this extended narrative from Exodus, the Hebrew leaders Moses and Aaron are consistently portrayed as servant-guides who act in the interests of the Hebrew people. When the Israelites face challenges (thirst at Marah, hunger in the wilderness, military threat from Amalek), Moses and Aaron respond by seeking God's help and providing solutions—not by antagonism. The leaders perform miracles, deliver manna, provide water, and establish systems of governance to serve the people. When people murmur or complain, the leaders address these concerns constructively. The antagonism evident in the text comes from Pharaoh and the Egyptians, not from the Hebrew leaders. Even when Moses questions the people rhetorically ('Why do you test the Lord?'), this represents exhortation rather than antagonism.
